document.title: Content Security Policy Header
document.content: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) is an HTTP response security header used to restrict which resources a browser is allowed to load. A missing CSP header may represent a security configuration weakness because CSP can reduce the impact of certain client-side attacks such as cross-site scripting. The absence of CSP should be distinguished from ordinary technology fingerprinting. Whether the finding is confirmed depends on whether the HTTP response evidence clearly demonstrates that the header is absent.

document.title: Missing HTTP Security Headers
document.content: HTTP security headers provide browser-side security controls. Examples include Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options and frame protection policies. A scanner may report missing security headers, but the evidence should identify which expected header is absent before a specific configuration weakness is considered confirmed. If the scanner reports missing headers while the stored evidence does not identify the missing header or otherwise demonstrate the configuration defect, additional review may be required.

document.title: Public API Documentation
document.content: Swagger UI, OpenAPI documents and ReDoc interfaces expose API documentation and endpoint metadata. Their presence can be useful for asset discovery and attack-surface mapping, but public API documentation is not automatically a vulnerability. Security impact depends on deployment context, exposed operations, authentication requirements and whether sensitive internal information is disclosed.

document.title: Prometheus Metrics Exposure
document.content: Prometheus metrics endpoints can expose runtime, process, application and infrastructure telemetry. If a metrics endpoint is accessible without intended access controls and returns operational metrics, the exposure may reveal information useful for reconnaissance or disclose sensitive operational details. The security impact depends on the content of the metrics and the intended accessibility of the endpoint.

document.title: Technology Detection
document.content: Technology detection identifies software products, frameworks, servers or other technologies used by a target. A confirmed technology fingerprint is generally an informational observation rather than direct evidence of a vulnerability. The detected technology may provide useful context for later vulnerability assessment, but technology identification alone does not demonstrate exploitability or a security defect.

document.title: CORS Misconfiguration
document.content: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) controls whether web resources can be accessed by scripts from other origins. A permissive CORS policy may become a security weakness when untrusted origins are allowed to read sensitive responses, especially when credentials or authenticated user data are involved. The presence of an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header alone does not confirm a vulnerability. Evidence should demonstrate the relevant origin policy, credential behavior, and whether sensitive resources can actually be accessed from an unintended origin. If these conditions are not shown, additional validation may be required.

document.title: Debug Interface Exposure
document.content: Debug interfaces and development endpoints may expose application internals, diagnostic information, environment details, stack traces or administrative functionality. A publicly reachable debug endpoint can represent an exposure when it returns operational or sensitive debugging information without intended access controls. Merely detecting a route or endpoint name is not sufficient to confirm the issue. Evidence should show that the endpoint is accessible and returns debugging information or functionality that was not intended for public access.

document.title: Sensitive File Exposure
document.content: Web-accessible sensitive files may disclose credentials, secrets, configuration values, source information or internal application details. Examples can include environment files, configuration backups, repository metadata and other files not intended for public access. A filename or HTTP route match alone does not prove sensitive information disclosure. Evidence should demonstrate that the file is accessible and that the returned content contains information that is actually sensitive or security-relevant. Empty, generic or unrelated responses may require additional review.

document.title: Directory Listing Exposure
document.content: Directory listing occurs when a web server exposes a browsable index of files and directories instead of serving an intended application page or denying access. This can reveal file names, directory structures, backups or other resources useful for reconnaissance. A directory path being reachable does not by itself confirm directory listing. Evidence should show an actual generated directory index or equivalent listing of server-side files. The security impact depends on the files and information exposed by the listing.

document.title: Default Credentials
document.content: Default credentials are vendor-provided, installation-default or commonly documented username and password combinations that remain valid on a deployed service. The existence of a login page, product fingerprint or known default credential pair does not by itself confirm that default credentials are active. Confirmation requires authorized evidence that the default credentials are accepted by the target or equivalent direct authentication evidence. Without authentication evidence, the finding should not be treated as a confirmed default-credential weakness.
